title: “HATE THE SIN, LOVE THE SINNER” — DID JESUS ACTUALLY SAY THIS?
paragraphs:
“HATE THE SIN, LOVE THE SINNER” — DID JESUS ACTUALLY SAY THIS?
Jesus never spoke those exact words. What He actually said is far more uncomfortable to the self-righteous, far more merciful to the broken, and far more powerful than the slogan we keep repeating.
There is a sentence Christians have repeated so often that many people assume it came straight from the mouth of Jesus:
It sounds like something Jesus could have said.
You can search the recorded words of Christ and you will not find Jesus saying, “Hate the sin, love the sinner.”
And before someone panics, this does not mean Christians are supposed to stop calling sin sin.
Jesus never softened sin into something harmless.
He spoke about adultery, hypocrisy, greed, lust, unbelief, unforgiveness, pride, and the corruption that comes from the human heart.
Jesus was not afraid of offending people with truth.
But here is where things become uncomfortable.
Jesus was also not afraid of offending religious people with grace.
And perhaps that is why this question matters more than we realize.
Because sometimes a sentence can contain an element of truth and still become a shield behind which we hide a heart that does not resemble Christ.
We say, “I hate the sin but love the sinner.”
In Matthew 5:44, the Greek text records:
Notice what Jesus does not say.
“Make sure they know how disgusted you are first.”
“Love the respectable sinners but despise the really bad ones.”
And suddenly Christianity stops being a slogan and becomes a cross.
Because anybody can love someone whose failures are socially acceptable to them.
Anybody can show mercy toward the sins they personally understand.
Anybody can be compassionate toward someone whose brokenness resembles their own.
But what happens when you encounter the person whose sin disgusts you?
What happens when their choices make you angry?
What happens when they have wounded people?
What happens when they represent everything you oppose?
What happens when the sinner is not somebody “out there” but your son?
That is where the slogan begins to crack open.
Because Christianity was never the story of righteous people standing safely at a distance from sinners.
Christianity is the story of a holy God coming near to them.
And if you are wondering how near...
He came close enough to be crucified.
There is something we must establish clearly.
Sin is not merely trauma, imperfection, personal preference, or an unfortunate mistake.
The New Testament commonly uses the Greek word ἁμαρτία — hamartia — for sin.
Scripture's diagnosis of humanity is devastatingly universal:
Not just whoever happens to be the target of Christian outrage this week.
That means before I point across the street...
I have to look into the mirror.
Before I speak about “the sinner,” I have to remember something Christianity will never allow me to forget:
I am talking about a category that includes me.

That does not erase meaningful distinctions between sins, consequences, victims, responsibilities, or earthly justice. Scripture does not teach that every sinful act produces identical earthly consequences.
But before the holiness of God, none of us gets to build our home on the moral high ground.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
And then comes the part we often forget.
Romans does not stop at verse 23.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not changing God's commandments whenever culture changes.
But guilty people being justified by grace because Someone else paid what they could never pay.
This is where Jesus destroys both cheap tolerance and loveless religion.
Grace does not say sin does not matter.
The cross says sin mattered enough for Christ to die.
But the cross also says the sinner mattered enough for Christ to come.
Think about Jesus at a dinner table.
Religious people noticed something scandalous about Him.
He kept eating with the wrong people.
People respectable religious society preferred to keep at arm's length.
Matthew 9 tells us that tax collectors and sinners were reclining at the table with Jesus and His disciples.
“Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”
There is an entire theology of superiority hidden inside that question.
Why is He so close to them?
Why does He sit with them?
Why doesn't He keep His distance?
Doesn't He know what kind of people they are?
And His response should still shake churches.
“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.”
Then He tells them to learn what this means:
“For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.”
Jesus is not saying sin is healthy.
His physician metaphor says precisely the opposite.
But doctors do not heal sick people by standing outside the hospital shouting about how disgusting disease is.
And His closeness was not approval.
That distinction desperately needs to return to Christian witness.
You can love someone without approving everything they do.
You can tell someone the truth without humiliating them.
You can call sin what God calls sin without treating the person trapped in it as though they are beyond redemption.
You can have biblical convictions without developing a Pharisee's heart.
Because the Gospel does not ask us to choose between truth and love.
Not fifty percent grace and fifty percent truth.
We often separate what Jesus perfectly held together.
He looks at sin with perfect holiness and at sinners with astonishing mercy.
And nobody demonstrates this more powerfully than Jesus Himself.
A man participating in a system notorious for exploitation.
Jesus sees him in a tree.
“Zacchaeus! Fix your life and maybe I'll speak to you afterward!”
Jesus says He must stay at his house.
“He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.”
But watch what happens when grace enters the house.
And Jesus declares that salvation has come to the house.
Then Jesus gives us one of the clearest descriptions of His mission:
“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
Not build an audience by raging at the lost.
And Christians should ask ourselves a painful question:
When sinners encounter us, do they feel the holiness of Christ calling them out of darkness...
or merely our disgust telling them they are unwanted?
Shame cannot resurrect the spiritually dead.
And the Gospel is not “become respectable enough that God will finally love you.”
The Gospel is that God acted toward us in Christ while we were still sinners.
Not sinners who finally had their theology perfectly organized.
Because if Christ waited until you deserved His love...
This is where “hate the sin, love the sinner” can become dangerous if we use it carelessly.

The problem is not necessarily the desire behind the phrase. Christians rightly understand that love does not require approving evil. Scripture itself commands believers to abhor evil and cling to what is good. Romans 12:9 says:
apostygountes to ponēron, kollōmenoi tō agathō
“Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good.”
We cannot rename darkness “light” simply to avoid offending someone.
We cannot celebrate what God calls sin and call that compassion.
But notice the same biblical context.
Romans 12 is overflowing with commands about genuine love, honoring others, patience, generosity, blessing persecutors, refusing vengeance, feeding enemies, overcoming evil with good.
Biblical hatred of evil was never permission to hate people.
And Jesus pushes this even further.
He commands love not merely for difficult people...
Because that is what the Father is like.
This is where the Gospel becomes painfully personal.
Maybe the person you have been calling “a sinner” is somebody Jesus is asking you to love.
Maybe you have technically defended biblical truth while quietly enjoying someone's humiliation.
Maybe you have reposted their scandal.
Smiled when somebody you disliked finally got exposed.
Maybe you know exactly which verses condemn somebody else's behavior...
but somehow keep skipping the verses confronting your bitterness.
That is the frightening thing about religious pride.
It can memorize Scripture while avoiding repentance.
It can defend holiness while secretly feeding hatred.
It can speak accurately about someone else's sin while remaining completely blind to its own.
Jesus told a story about that too.
A Pharisee and a tax collector entered the temple to pray.
The Pharisee essentially thanked God that he was not like other people.
The tax collector could barely lift his eyes.
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
ho Theos, hilastheti moi tō hamartōlō
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
And Jesus says the tax collector went home justified.
The broken man knew something the religious man had forgotten.
Maybe that is what some of us have forgotten.
We became Christians long enough ago that we forgot what it felt like to need rescue.
We learned what Christians should condemn.
we forgot the pit Christ pulled us from.
And grace did not stay dead.
This is why the Gospel Warrior theme matters so deeply:
Jesus does not rewrite God's definition of sin to make us comfortable.
He rewrites the sinner's story through redemption.
He does not tell darkness that it was light all along.
He brings us out of darkness.
He does not tell the guilty that guilt is imaginary.
He does not tell captives that their chains are beautiful.
He does not merely improve sinners.
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
And that means there is something even more important than asking:
“Did Jesus say, ‘Hate the sin, love the sinner’?”
How did Jesus actually love sinners?
He came near without becoming corrupted by their sin.
He told truth without surrendering compassion.
He offered mercy without pretending repentance was unnecessary.
So maybe instead of spending our lives repeating a sentence Jesus never said, we should spend our lives obeying the sentences He actually did say.
“Judge not, that you be not judged.”
“Whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them.”
Jesus does not save us so we can comfortably remain enslaved to what destroys us.
Grace is not God's permission slip for sin.
Grace is God's rescue of sinners.
Titus 2 says the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness.
Real grace sometimes wounds our pride before healing our hearts.
And perhaps this article is doing that to somebody right now.
Maybe you opened this expecting ammunition against somebody else's sin.
And somehow Jesus turned the mirror toward you.
Maybe the sin you need to hate today is not theirs.
Your refusal to forgive the person who wounded you.
Maybe you have spent years pointing at the darkness in everyone else because looking at your own became unbearable.
The thing nobody at church knows?
The thoughts you would be terrified for anybody else to hear.
And He is still calling you.
This is where conviction becomes beautiful.
Because the hand exposing the wound is the hand pierced to heal you.
Jesus did not go to Calvary because you were almost good enough.
He went because you could never save yourself.
At the cross, God's hatred of sin and God's love toward sinners are not cheap slogans.
They become blood and wood and nails and mercy.
And the sinner who comes to Christ empty-handed discovers something astonishing:
There is a new beginning here.
There is no scandal too filthy for the blood of Jesus to cleanse when a sinner truly turns to Him.
No past so permanent that Christ cannot redeem it.
No chain stronger than His power.
No grave deeper than His resurrection.
That does not mean earthly consequences magically disappear.
It does not mean victims should be forced into unsafe situations.
It does not mean justice becomes unnecessary.
It does not mean repentance is merely saying sorry.
Biblical grace is not pretending nothing happened.
Grace is God doing what we could never do for ourselves and transforming those who belong to Christ.
So if you are reading this while carrying a secret...
If you have wandered from Jesus...
If shame convinced you God could never receive you...
If you have been using truth as a weapon instead of carrying it with tears...
If you have been calling evil good because you feared rejection...
Every road eventually arrives at the same place.
All of us standing before the cross with empty hands.
And maybe the most Christlike way to say “hate the sin, love the sinner” is not to say it at all.
Maybe it is to live something deeper:
Forgive as you have been forgiven.
And never forget that you stand by grace.
If this exposed something you have been hiding behind religion, do not perform for anybody.
Sometimes the beginning of freedom is finally refusing to hide.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
There may come a day when somebody you love confesses something that shocks you, and before you react, you may need to remember how Jesus dealt with sinners...
and how Jesus dealt with you.
It does not. The Gospel cannot be bought, salvation cannot be purchased, and God's grace is not for sale.
If you have received something spiritually valuable here, help put it in front of somebody who may never search for it themselves.
Are you trusting Him rather than your own goodness?
Because one day you will not stand before God holding a Christian slogan.
You will stand before Him needing a Savior.
The question was, “Hate the sin, love the sinner—did Jesus actually say this?”
And then He stretched out His arms on a cross and demonstrated just how far holy love was willing to go to rescue sinners like us.
You were never the scandal Jesus was afraid to touch—you were the sinner He was willing to bleed to redeem.
